Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0 highlights culture as a pillar of European security Courtesy of the Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0 Participants of the Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0 gather in Warsaw on May 7-8. The forum brought together museum professionals, diplomats and cultural experts from seven countries for discussions on protecting Ukrainian cultural heritage during wartime. Thessaloniki, Greece – Ukrainian museum officials, diplomats, cultural leaders and Kyiv’s European partners gathered in Warsaw on May 7-8 for the Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0, a major international event focused on protecting national cultural heritage during wartime and strengthening what organizers increasingly describe as Europe’s cultural security. Hosted by the OBMIN Foundation with the participation of the embassies of Germany and Ukraine in Poland, the forum brought together some 160 experts and officials from seven countries. Participants discussed the preservation of Ukraine’s cultural heritage amid Russia’s ongoing attacks, the role of museums in fighting disinformation, and how culture has become intertwined with questions of national security, democratic resilience and postwar recovery. The event was a continuation of a series of conferences launched by the OBMIN network after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Organizers framed the forum as both a response to the destruction caused by the war and a platform for building long-term international partnerships around culture and identity. “Culture is not a luxury – it is a front line,” OBMIN said in a statement opening the forum. Organizers stressed that Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine for territorial conquest but also to systematically destroy Ukrainian culture, history and national identity. The first day of the conference took place at the German Embassy in Warsaw and focused on discussions about “weaponized culture,” disinformation campaigns, and the role of museums as “guardians of identity.” The second day moved to PANOPTIKUM, a newly built museum resource center near Warsaw developed by Poland’s National Institute for Museums. Participants examined technical approaches to preserving collections during wartime, including secure storage systems, emergency logistics and restoration tools and techniques. Delegates also visited the Warsaw Gas Museum as part of discussions about industrial heritage and museum resilience. Ukraine’s First Deputy Minister of Culture Ivan Verbytskyi participated in the forum and emphasized the importance of international partnerships for Ukraine’s cultural sector during wartime. “Establishing partnerships and exchanging experience for Ukraine is an opportunity to attract assistance in conditions of limited resources,” Mr. Verbytskyi said. “For international partners, it is an opportunity to study experience in responding and adapting to the challenges of war.” One of the forum’s central topics was international support for the Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Fund, a multi-donor platform created to finance the restoration of Ukrainian cultural heritage damaged or threatened during the war. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture, the fund was established last year and registered in Brussels under European legislation. Its co-founders include Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture, represented by the Ukrainian Center for Cultural Research, and the ALIPH Foundation, an international organization specializing in the protection of endangered cultural heritage. Mr. Verbytskyi also participated in a panel titled “Guardians of Identity: How Museums Define Resistance and Resilien­ce.” Discussions focused on countering disinformation, strengthening sovereignty through culture, and expanding international cultural diplomacy during wartime. Several speakers argued that Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s museums, archives and monuments should not be viewed as accidents, but rather as part of a broader Kremlin strategy aimed at erasing Ukrainian identity. “Genocide is not just the physical extermination of a people; it is the systematic destruction of their culture, history and identity,” organizers said in one of the forum’s opening statements. Mykyta Poturaiev, chair of the humanitarian and information policy committee in Ukraine’s parliament, addressed the forum via a video message. “Russia is attempting to kill the very essence of what makes us human,” Mr. Poturaiev said. Ukraine’s Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Olexandr Mischenko participated in a panel titled “False Past, Stolen Future? Disinformation, Culture as a Weapon and the Struggle for Truth,” where he argued that Russian propaganda has become one of Moscow’s primary instruments of war. “Disinformation has long become a component of Russian state policy and one of the key instruments of war against Ukraine and the democratic world,” Mr. Mischenko wrote after the forum. He warned that Russia systematically uses information campaigns to undermine trust in democratic institutions, polarize societies and weaken international support for Ukraine. Mr. Mischenko also drew historical parallels between contemporary Russian rhetoric and propaganda used by Nazi Germa­ny before World War II. “Denial of a people’s right to their own history, culture and statehood has always been a characteristic feature of dictatorial regimes,” he said. According to Mr. Mischenko, Russia continues to portray Ukraine as an “artificial state” without a distinct national identity while simultaneously targeting Ukrainian museums, archives and cultural institutions. He also highlighted Russian information operations aimed at creating tension between Ukrainians and Poles by manipulating historical issues, migration debates and isolated social conflicts. At the same time, the deputy foreign affairs minister thanked Poland and the Polish citizenry for its continued support despite what he described as large-scale Russian disinformation attacks. Participants repeatedly emphasized that Ukraine’s experience in resisting disinformation has become increasingly relevant for the rest of Europe. “Protection of the information space has become an integral component of the security of democratic societies,” Mr. Mischenko said, adding that propaganda and disinformation should be treated “as a full-fledged instrument of aggression alongside military means.” The forum also highlighted the growing role of museums in documenting war, preserving memory and strengthening social resilience. The OBMIN Foundation itself was established shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 as a platform for connecting Ukrainian museums with European partners. The organization currently represents 156 museums across Ukraine, ranging from major national institutions in Kyiv to regional museums focused on local history and culture. According to OBMIN, the network initially focused on emergency assistance and survival support for museums and museum employees during wartime. It later expanded into professional exchanges, digitization initiatives and international cultural projects aimed at promoting knowledge about Ukrainian culture abroad. Representatives of Ukrainian cultural institutions called the forum an important international platform for dialogue and cooperation. Officials from the Andrey Sheptytsky National Museum in Lviv said the gathering united experts and cultural representatives “to discuss the role of culture and the formation of a security system during an existential war.” Franko House in Lviv described the forum as a space for discussing “the role of culture during war and challenges related to preserving cultural heritage, historical memory and national identity.” International museum organizations also participated in the event. The Network of European Museum Organizations (NEMO) contributed to discussions about museum security standards and emergency preparedness. According to NEMO, Poland’s museum sector has significantly expanded its work since Russia’s full-scale invasion, providing humanitarian assistance, training and crisis-preparedness guidance for museums operating under wartime conditions. The Ukraine Culture Security Forum was also presented as a precursor to broader international discussions about reconstruction and recovery. Organizers linked the event to discussions held at the Ukraine Recovery Conference and argued that cultural preservation must become part of Europe’s long-term rebuilding strategy. For many participants, the discussions in Warsaw reflected a broader shift in how European institutions are increasingly understanding culture – not as a secondary issue during wartime, but as a central element of sovereignty, democratic resilience and collective security. “In response to Russia’s attempts to falsify history and manipulate the past,” Mr. Mischenko said, “democratic societies must respond with unity, resilience and systematic protection of truth.” Premium Previous Article Ukraine seeks European role in proposed ‘airport ceasefire’ with Russia Next Article Ukrainian drone strikes deep in Russia grow public alarm Related Posts Britain’s new prime minister reaffirms support for Ukraine in first meeting with Zelenskyy July 31, 2026 1:38 am By Roman Tymotsko Breaking News Deadly strike on defense technology event forces Ukraine to rethink industry gatherings July 31, 2026 1:33 am By Roman Tymotsko Ukraine Olena Teliha remembered as Ukraine marks 120th anniversary of her birth July 31, 2026 1:27 am By Roman Tymotsko Ukraine Comments are closed. Adri Salido/Getty Images Add Fortune on Google for similar content. Add us on Google Add us on Google Spain on Saturday installed a 500-meter-long (1,600-foot) barrier on the sea border between its North African territory of Ceuta and neighboring Morocco after tens of thousands of migrants breached the frontier earlier in the week. Recommended Video At least 67 migrants died, including some who drowned and others who were killed in a stampede to cross a breakwater barrier , the Spanish government said Saturday. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez slammed the reaction of some other European Union leaders to the events in Ceuta , saying calls for Spain to be suspended from the EU’s borderless Schengen zone were “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest.” A handful of exhausted migrants who swam to Ceuta’s urban Tarajal beach Saturday morning were met by soldiers who escorted them across the border. Most of the 50,000 to 60,000 migrants who entered the territory between Thursday and Friday soon went back. “We are relentless against those who break the law,” Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told journalists Saturday. Questioned how the massive border breach could have happened given the heavy security on both sides of the border and whether Morocco posed a threat to Ceuta, Marlaska defended the government in Rabat. “The events require an evaluation by Spain and Morocco,” he said. But it was the cooperation with its neighbors that allowed Spain “to revert the situation in 24 hours.” “Morocco is not a threat to Ceuta, or to the rest of Spain. It is a reliable partner,” Marlaska emphasized. EU leaders call for coordinated response The leaders of 22 EU countries called for a coordinated response to the situation. In a letter to top EU officials, released Saturday by the Danish prime minister’s office, the countries asked the EU’s current Irish presidency to urgently convene a videoconference of interior ministers. “We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalization of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” the letter said. “Such a perception would encourage further attempts, undermine confidence in our common migration policy and have repercussions for all Member States.” Leaders of Italy, Denmark, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia and Sweden signed the letter. Sánchez also asked for a videoconference of EU interior ministers to “enable us to establish a common response to situations of this kind and reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all Member States, and not only of those on the Union’s front line.” Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni has threatened to suspend Italy’s open-border Schengen agreement with Spain, and Italy was reimposing border controls for people arriving from Spain by air and sea. “In the current international context, the European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarizing and unlawful reaction,” Sánchez wrote in his letter. Migrants head back into Morocco Hundreds of migrants returned to Morocco on Saturday. Some told an Associated Press reporter they were returning “of their own free will” after what they described as degrading treatment on the Spanish side of the border. Migrants walked along a long stretch of wave breakers before slipping into Morocco through a small breach in the border fence that had become an informal entry point. Moroccan police and soldiers watched. Most of the migrants were Moroccans, while a smaller number were from sub-Saharan Africa. Hungry and angry, some barefoot or shirtless and others nursing visible injuries, those who returned said they had “seen hell in Ceuta.” “I decided to come back on my own,” said Ouail Lamzeiz. “I spent eight days in Ceuta, and I was about to get a bed at the migrant center, but I hadn’t eaten for days. Even the Moroccans there didn’t help,” he added, showing a document supporting his account. His friend, Salah Eddine El Arrage, said he decided to return to Morocco after, he said, Spanish police beat him. Migrants said they spent their nights sleeping in the forests around Ceuta because they could not find shelter, and that they often fought over food. One, Othmane El Merzoug, asked passersby for a phone call so he could reach his family and ask them to send money for the journey back to his hometown, about 189 miles (305 kilometers) from the border. Along Ceuta’s Tarajal beach, sunbathers largely ignored the streams of migrants walking toward the border. Ceuta resident Mohamed Abdelatif, 21, said the border rush had ruptured the city’s peace. “The reality is, it’s not good,” Abdelatif said, before wading into the water with his girlfriend. The road linking the Moroccan town of Fnideq to the border crossing bore the scars of the unrest. Burned-out vehicles sat along the roadside, while the acrid smell of smoke still hung in the air. Police barriers channeled traffic toward the crossing, and water cannons remained stationed nearby. “Life in this city has been disrupted as a result of the border incident,” said Ceuta President Juan Jesús Vivas. “The return of people has begun satisfactorily but the process must be completed.” In the Moroccan city of Tangier, about 75 kilometers (46 miles) west of Ceuta, the main railway station was busy with people returning. Some slept on the ground. “I tried to cross, but I failed. I stayed near the border with Ceuta for two days, but I couldn’t find anything to eat,” said Abdalah, an aspiring migrant who asked that his last name not be published out of fear of retaliation for trying to cross illegally. But some who made it to Ceuta were determined to stay. Among them was Mohamed Hatri, a 23-year-old Moroccan. “They’ve closed everything down so that we can’t buy anything to eat, to force us to return to our country,” he said, adding that he and others were determined to stay “whether we’re hungry or not.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. (AP Photo/Anthony Pizzoferrato) (Anthony Pizzoferrato/AP Photo/Anthony Pizzoferrato) By AVET DEMOURIAN and YURAS KARMANAU, Associated Press August 07, 2026 at 1:25 pm EDT YEREVAN, Armenia — The head of the influential Armenian Apostolic Church appeared in court Friday for a trial on criminal charges as part of its latest confrontation with the government of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Catholicos Karekin II and six other senior clergymen are accused of defying a court order to reinstate a defrocked bishop. The case is widely seen as a part of long-simmering tensions between Pashinyan, who was reelected earlier this year, and the church, which has called for his ouster. If convicted, Karekin and the other clerics could face up to two years in prison. Relations between the powerful church and Pashinyan's government have deteriorated rapidly since 2024, when tens of thousands of demonstrators , led by a high-ranking cleric, called for his ouster. They were angered by Armenia's agreement to hand over control of several border villages to Azerbaijan and normalize relations with its neighbor after being locked for decades in territorial disputes. Many clergy bitterly opposed the handover of the villages and criticized Pashinyan, who came to power in the South Caucasus nation amid a wave of hopeful, pro-democracy protests that swept Armenia in 2018. Some senior clerics have since faced a crackdown by the government. The judge in the trial recuses himself The first court hearing took place Friday in the central city of Vagharshapat, also known as Etchmiadzin, which is Armenia's spiritual capital and the headquarters of the church. Shortly after the hearing, Karekin's lawyer Ara Zograbyan told reporters the judge in the case has recused himself. “I welcome this move by the judge, because in effect he refused to become a part of this shameful proceeding,”Zograbyan said, adding that the case will be assigned to a new judge. Hundreds of Karekin's supporters gathered outside the courthouse in Vagharshapat, which is located about 18 kilometers (11 miles) west of Armenia's capital, Yerevan. Members of opposition parties, clergy leaders and representatives of nongovernmental organizations also came for the hearing. Samvel Karapetyan, head of the pro-Russian opposition party Strong Armenia, called the case against Karekin a “national disgrace.” “It seemed that maybe the authorities would come to their senses and stop their attacks on the church, but they're keeping at it,” local media quoted him as saying. The case of a defrocked bishop led to the charges The charges arose after the church in January defrocked Bishop Gevorg Saroyan, who had previously called for Karekin's ouster. The church accused Saroyan of abuse of power. Saroyan contested the move in court, which sided with him and ordered his reinstatement. The church refused, and Armenia's Prosecutor General's office launched the case against Karekin and the other clerics in February, accusing them of defying a court order and barring them from leaving the country. Two other top clergymen were arrested last year. Archbishop Mikael Ajapahyan was convicted of calling for the overthrow of the government, and Archbishop Bagrat Galstanyan , who led the anti-government protests in 2024, is currently under house arrest awaiting trial on charges of attempting a coup, fomenting mass unrest and preparing a terrorist attack. Earlier this year, an appellate court overturned Ajapahyan's conviction and ordered a new trial. Clerics denounce the case as an assault on church autonomy During an evening service at the Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Karekin denounced the case against him. “These days the authorities take steps to undermine the church's authority, restrict its autonomy and subjugate it to their will,” he said, adding that the institution's autonomy is at the core of Armenia's prosperity. Archbishop Natan Hovhannisyan, head of the Department of External Relations and Protocol of the church and one of the defendants, said the church is not an entity that can be “nationalized, expropriated and have a manager appointed.” —- Karmanau reported from Tallinn, Estonia. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c54g.text: Image source, Saudi Hospital medics Image caption, Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed By Barbara Plett Usher ,Â Africa correspondent Â and Â Mohamed Madi Published 3 hours ago A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago. UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings. The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation. Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times. Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict. The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted. "The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC. "The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned." The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military. Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities. In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility. But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query. UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city. The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city. A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan Published 13 November 2025 Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past Published 31 October 2025 Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023. Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city. Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies. The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher. In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city. The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman. The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says. On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added. The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist. But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office. They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs. "There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners. Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead. "They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me." That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said. The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated. Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base. According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy". In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim. He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters. Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war. The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges. After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases. Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) sounded the alarm. "We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, butâ¦ the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement. However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting. They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks. Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics. Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked. The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close. Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated. By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left. The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened. Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building. They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased. Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025. In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed. In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived. "From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said. Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients. On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says. It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people. On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC. It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says. Image source, El-Fasher Resistance Committee Image caption, The burnt-out ruins of a building in a compound that housed a medical warehouse and dialysis centre in el-Fasher pictured after it was hit by a missile The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces. "Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said. Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients. The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions . The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital. The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office. "Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," TÃ¼rk said. Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients. Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work. "I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them. "We liberated them," he said. The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there. "If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head." He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed. They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital. "They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera. A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp. The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v.text: Image source, US Government / Handout via REUTERS Image caption, Stephen Hubbard (second from left in the first row) was flown back home on a US plane earlier this week By Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent in Kyiv Published 41 minutes ago Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention. Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022. "We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days." Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers. "It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read." Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner. He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial. Image source, Courtesy of Ihor Shyshko Image caption, Ihor Shyshko alleges that Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of Russian prison staff Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun. "They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold. "He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'." Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff. Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison. The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine. Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine. US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before. Image source, Francesco Tosto / BBC Image caption, Dmytro Khyliuk says Hubbard was hidden in a Russian prison to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv. He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor. Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth. "It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said. Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened. "There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said. "Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move." They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions. "There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said. Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors. "I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said. The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue." Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange. He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. "Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners". Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US. "I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said. But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress". Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice. "Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".
